# White-Bear Steering: Steering Toward a "Think About It" Stance Makes Implied Concepts Readable in J-Space

Priya Raman, Tomasz Wierzbicki, Elise Fournier
Orrery Lab

*Preprint, 6 October 2026. Comments welcome.*

---

## Abstract

Jacobian-lens (J-lens) readouts surface what a model is internally "holding" at a position, but concepts that a
text only implies (a chess game described without the word *chess*) are often buried thousands of ranks down. We
ask whether a single, concept-agnostic steering vector can lift them. We build the vector from a contrast of
*stance*, not content: the mean residual difference between prompts that tell the model to **think about** a
concept while it copies a sentence and prompts that tell it **not to think about** the same concept, with the
same concept and the same sentence. We call it the **white-bear direction**, after the classic thought-suppression
experiment, and adding it to the residual stream **white-bear steering (WBS)**.

On Qwen3.5-4B and WorkspaceBench's association family, WBS at layers 20-24 raises strict pass@10 after the
steered band (layers 26-30) from 0.14 to 0.83 (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]; 68 items gained, 0 lost), and over all read
layers from 0.33 to 0.88. In the clearest case, *chess* rises from rank 1,210 to rank 9. A random direction at the
same dose does nothing. Gains on other families are small. The effect needs a large dose and a narrow one: below
about two units it is invisible, which may be why stance steering has not been reported before, and it peaks
sharply at six. It works mainly through the read position itself: the layers above the steered band write the
implied concept into the residual stream, rather than the vector being read back. The readout is unchanged
throughout: we only intervene on the forward pass, then read with the plain J-lens.

## 1 Introduction

Lens methods decode a transformer's intermediate states into vocabulary space. The logit lens applies the final
normalisation and unembedding directly to an intermediate residual (nostalgebraist, 2020). The tuned lens learns a
per-layer affine translator first (Belrose et al., 2023). Patchscopes decode by patching the state into a second
forward pass (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024). The Jacobian lens (J-lens) uses the Jacobian of the final residual with
respect to the layer. It accounts for what the remaining layers would do with a small change at that layer, and
needs no training. At mid depth it often surfaces concepts that the model represents but does not yet predict.

WorkspaceBench (WSB) turns this into a measurement. Each item is a prompt, a read position and a set of target
tokens. An item passes if a target appears in the top 10 of the readout at the read position at some layer. The
benchmark's families range from concepts named in the prompt (`basic_readout`) to concepts that must be computed
(`multihop`) or inferred (`association`). The association family is the hardest for the J-lens. A typical prompt
evokes a concept without naming it:

> "Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
> looking up."

The target, *chess*, must appear in the top 10 at the final prompt token. On Qwen3.5-4B under the plain J-lens,
only 33% of scored association items pass at any read layer, and 14% after layer 26.

There are two readings of such a failure. Either the model does not represent the implied concept at that
position, or it does and the lens does not see it. Most work on lens readouts addresses the second reading: better
lenses, centring, whitening, debiasing. We take the first reading seriously and keep the readout fixed. Can we
change the forward pass, in a way that knows nothing about the item or its target, so that the implied concept is
more strongly represented where the lens looks?

Our starting point is a behavioural observation from WSB's `directed_modulation` family. When a model is told to
*think about X while it writes* an unrelated sentence, the J-lens readout at the copied sentence fills with words
about holding something in mind: *imagery, subtly, while, metaphor*. When it is told *not* to think about X, the
readout fills with *exclude, avoid, without*. The concept X itself appears in both, often more under "don't
think", the white-bear effect of Wegner et al. (1987) in miniature. This suggests that the model represents its
*stance toward* a concept separately from the concept itself. If so, the stance direction might work as a generic
amplifier. Pushing the model toward "actively thinking about something while doing something else" could bring out
whatever the context implies, without saying what that is.

This is what we find, with two surprises. First, the dose that works is large by the standards of activation
steering: in total about as large as the residual norm at the read cells, spread over five layers. Conventional
doses fall in a flat region of the dose curve, and the useful region is narrow. Second, the vector is not read
back. Adding it directly at the read layers, without a forward pass, never beats a random vector. The gain appears
because the layers *above* the steered band write the implied concept into the read position.

**Contributions.**
1. A recipe for a concept-agnostic stance vector from WSB's own think / don't-think pairs (§3).
2. Evidence that steering along it at mid depth makes implied concepts more readable through the plain J-lens,
   against a matched random control and across a dose curve (§5).
3. Ablations of depth, positions and contrast, showing that the effect needs the band at layers 20-24, works mostly
   through the read position, and is specific to the think / don't-think contrast (§5.5-5.7).
4. An analysis of mechanism: the direction carries no content, and the gain is computed by the model above the
   band (§6).

## 2 Background

### 2.1 The J-lens readout

For a residual state $h_l$ at layer $l$, the J-lens score of token $v$ is

$$ s_l(v) = \frac{\langle W_U[v],\, J_l h_l \rangle}{\lVert J_l^{\top} W_U[v] \rVert}, $$

where $J_l$ is the input-averaged Jacobian of the final residual with respect to $h_l$ and $W_U$ the unembedding.
This is WSB's cosine readout. We rank the full vocabulary by $s_l$ and take the top 10.

### 2.2 WorkspaceBench

WSB pins Qwen3.6-27B and a public J-lens for it. We run its items and its scorer unchanged on a smaller model
(§4). Each family specifies how the read positions are chosen. For `association` it is the final prompt token,
read on the 27B at layers 4, 8, ..., 60; on the 4B we read at the same relative depths, layers 2, 4, ..., 30.
Scoring is strict: a top-10 token must equal an accepted target token. Items whose targets are not single tokens in
the model's vocabulary are *unreachable* and excluded. WSB reports pass@10 over layers 20-60 of the 27B (layers
10-30 of the 4B). We also report the window after our intervention (§3.3).

### 2.3 Activation steering

Activation addition adds a vector to the residual stream during the forward pass (Turner et al., 2023).
Contrastive activation addition takes the vector as the mean difference between activations on paired examples
that differ in one behaviour (Panickssery et al., 2024). Such vectors move behaviours that the model represents as
a direction, such as refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), sycophancy or truthfulness (Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023).
Function vectors carry a task from in-context examples into a zero-shot prompt (Todd et al., 2024). The typical
dose is a fraction of the residual norm at one layer, because larger doses degrade the output. Steering vectors are
usually evaluated by their effect on behaviour. Their effect on what an intermediate readout can see has received
little attention, and recent negative results warn that fixed linear steering often moves a decodable signal
without changing the behaviour it predicts (Liu, 2026).

## 3 Method

### 3.1 The white-bear direction

WSB's `directed_modulation` family contains 35 *pair* items. In each pair, the same concept and the same carrier
sentence appear under two instructions:

> **think:** Think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence: "The committee
> approved the minutes without changes."
>
> **don't think:** Do not think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence:
> "The committee approved the minutes without changes."

Instruction wordings vary across pairs, e.g. "Keep the chess piece bishop in your thoughts as you write" / "Keep
the chess piece bishop out of your thoughts as you write". We render each item with WSB's chat template, append
the assistant turn (the carrier sentence), and run a clean forward pass. At each layer `l`, we average the residual
states over each prompt's **carrier cells** (WSB's `writing_positions` read cells: the tokens of the copied
sentence in the assistant turn), then average per condition:

    d_l = mean_{think}(h_l) - mean_{don't think}(h_l)          per-prompt carrier means, all 35 pairs
    u_l = d_l / ||d_l||

The concept and the carrier are matched within each pair, so they cancel. Only the stance remains. The direction
is stable: leave-one-pair-out versions have cosine >= 0.997 with the full one at every layer from 20 to 24. It also
separates the conditions it was not fitted on. Projected onto `u_22`, held-out WSB `directed_modulation` items with
"think" instructions score higher than their "don't think" counterparts with AUC 0.97.

### 3.2 Steering

During the forward pass on an evaluation item, we add the direction at the output of every block in a band of
layers, at every position of the prompt up to and including the read position:

    h_l  <-  h_l + k * s_l * u_l          for l in {20, 21, 22, 23, 24}

Here `k` is the **dose** and `s_l` a fixed per-layer step (Table A1): 0.13 `||d_l||`, the think / don't-think gap
at that layer scaled once for all layers. The residual stream accumulates, so a dose of `k` adds about `3.4 k`
along the direction by layer 24. At our best dose, `k = 6`, that is about 20, comparable to the median residual
norm at the read cells of layers 20-24 (17-58, Table A1). Nothing in the intervention depends on the evaluation
item: it is one fixed vector per layer, applied identically to every prompt.

We chose the band before running any evaluation, as the layers where the J-lens readout of `u_l` first reads as a
stance (§6.1). We revisit it in §5.5.

### 3.3 Readout and scoring

We read with the plain J-lens (WSB's cosine readout), with no centring or other change, at WSB's read cell and
layers. We use WSB's strict pass@10 on the bench split and report two windows:

- **all layers** (L10-30), WSB's own window at the 4B's depth;
- **after the band** (L26-30), the layers downstream of the intervention. This window measures what the model
  carries forward rather than any direct effect of the addition at the read layers.

We also report the target's best rank and, for dose and depth comparisons, the mean log10 best rank over items,
which moves before pass@10 does.

## 4 Setup

- **Model:** Qwen3.5-4B (32 layers), thinking off, bf16 weights. Interventions are computed in fp32 and cast back.
  We use the 4B rather than WSB's pinned 27B so that full dose curves fit on one small GPU.
- **Lens:** the public J-lens for Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Evaluation:** WSB association, bench split (100 items, 98 scorable). For transfer, seven other WSB families
  (§5.4).
- **Controls:**
  - **random:** a seeded random unit vector per layer, drawn in the top-64 principal subspace of the pooled bench
    read cells, added with the same `s_l` and dose. Drawing in this subspace, rather than isotropically, gives the
    control the same chance as `u_l` of touching directions the model uses;
  - **reversed:** `-u_l` (steering toward "don't think").
- **Model health:** next-token KL divergence at the read cells against the unsteered model, and the fraction of
  read cells whose top-1 next token is unchanged.
- **Intervals:** 95% paired bootstrap over items (5,000 resamples).
- **Compute:** one 24 GB GPU; a full dose curve over eight families takes about forty minutes.

## 5 Results

### 5.1 Main result

| association (n = 98), strict pass@10 | all layers (L10-30) | after the band (L26-30) |
|---|---|---|
| plain J-lens, no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| WBS, k = 4 | 0.42 | 0.29 |
| **WBS, k = 6** | **0.88** (+0.55 [+0.45, +0.64]) | **0.83** (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]) |
| random direction, k = 6 | 0.31 (-0.02) | 0.14 (+0.00 [-0.03, +0.03]) |

At `k = 6`, WBS gains 68 items after the band and loses none. The random direction at the same dose gains one and
loses one. Over all layers, WBS gains 54 and loses none.

The items gained after the band include *golf, tennis, avalanche, piano, baseball, fire, library, pizza, rain,
volcano, chess, desert, noir, poker* (Appendix C). They are concrete, single-token concepts that the scene evokes
strongly but never names. Of the 17 scorable items that stay unread, most start far down the unsteered readout
(*archery, opera, submarine, lighthouse*; §6.3).

### 5.2 The dose curve and its cost

| dose k | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | **6** | 7 | 8 | 12 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pass@10, all layers | 0.33 | 0.33 | 0.35 | 0.36 | 0.42 | 0.55 | **0.88** | 0.74 | 0.56 | 0.19 | 0.12 |
| pass@10, after band | 0.14 | 0.15 | 0.19 | 0.21 | 0.29 | 0.45 | **0.83** | 0.65 | 0.43 | 0.02 | 0.00 |
| next-token KL | 0.005 | 0.02 | 0.06 | 0.13 | 0.21 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.52 | 0.63 | 1.22 | 2.01 |
| top-1 unchanged | 0.90 | 0.87 | 0.82 | 0.73 | 0.68 | 0.61 | 0.56 | 0.51 | 0.44 | 0.35 | 0.10 |

Doses at or below 1 do nothing measurable. The gain then grows slowly to `k = 4`, steeply to a peak at `k = 6`,
and falls again past 7. At 12 and beyond, the steering rewrites the readout wholesale and the model's own
next-token prediction changes at most read cells; pass@10 drops below the baseline. Reversed steering at `k = 1`
gives 0.32 / 0.12, slightly below baseline.

**We stress the dose.** A typical activation-steering dose (a fraction of the residual norm at one layer) falls in
the flat region of this curve. Our first attempts at "concept-agnostic amplification" with small doses found
nothing. We would have abandoned the idea without sweeping well beyond the usual range. The peak is also narrow:
`k = 5` and `k = 7` keep only about half and three-quarters of the gain after the band.

**The cost is real but bounded.** At the peak, the next-token distribution at the read cell moves by a KL of 0.40
on association, and the top-1 token changes at about 44% of read cells. A random direction at the same dose moves
it by only 0.06: the model is sensitive to the white-bear direction specifically. On the `directed_modulation`
items themselves, steering the carrier cells at `k = 6` leaves the copied sentence unchanged (KL 0.001). The model
goes on copying exactly, while its internal readout changes.

### 5.3 Examples

*"Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
looking up."* Target: **chess**.

| | best rank of *chess* (L26-30) | J-lens top 10 at layer 30 |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 1,210 | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, He, In |
| WBS, k = 6 | **9** | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, **chess**, He |
| random, k = 6 | 1,140 | <\|im_end\|>, \n\n, forty, The, They, She, His, It, “, He |

The steered readout keeps the generic continuation tokens. The implied concept joins them. The best rank of
*chess* falls smoothly with the dose: 1,210 (k ≤ 1), 456 (k = 2), 172 (k = 3), 65 (k = 4), 24 (k = 5), 9 (k = 6),
and back to 24 at k = 8. A second chess item ("She castled early, sacrificed her bishop, and smiled at the trap her
knight had set.") goes from rank 4 to rank 2.

### 5.4 Other families

Strict pass@10, all layers / after the band, no steering vs WBS at `k = 4` and `k = 6` (random `k = 6` in the
last column):

| family | n | no steering | WBS k = 4 | WBS k = 6 | random k = 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| association | 98 | 0.33 / 0.14 | 0.42 / 0.29 | **0.88 / 0.83** | 0.31 / 0.14 |
| multihop | 94 | 0.58 / 0.50 | 0.60 / 0.53 | 0.62 / 0.56 | 0.57 / 0.48 |
| typo | 100 | 0.41 / 0.07 | 0.42 / 0.09 | 0.44 / 0.11 | 0.40 / 0.06 |
| user_modeling | 50 | 0.30 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.24 | 0.28 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.22 |
| brew_intermediates | 100 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 |
| chain_intermediates | 114 | 0.47 / 0.44 | 0.48 / 0.41 | 0.46 / 0.40 | 0.47 / 0.44 |
| basic_readout | 68 | 0.88 / 0.87 | 0.90 / 0.90 | 0.91 / 0.90 | 0.88 / 0.87 |
| multilingual | 100 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 |

The gain is concentrated in association. Multihop and typo (whose targets are the intended words behind
misspellings) gain a little after the band (0.50 → 0.56, 0.07 → 0.11). Families near ceiling do not move. Chain
intermediates lose a little after the band. Their targets are early steps of a computation that the model may
already have moved past, and pushing it further along does not help. We do not know why association benefits so
much more than multihop on this model; its targets are mostly concrete scene concepts that the unsteered model
already ranks within a few hundred (§6.3).

### 5.5 Depth

Is the band at layers 20-24 special? We move the same five-layer band through the network, keeping the dose at
`k = 4` (with `s_l` = 0.13 `||d_l||` at each layer, as in §3.2), and read association after it at layers 26-30.
We report the change in mean log10 best rank against no steering (negative is better):

| band | L2-6 | L8-12 | L14-18 | **L20-24** | L26-30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WBS, Δ mean log10 rank | -0.01 | +0.02 | -0.14 | **-0.95** | +0.03 |

Only the band at layers 20-24 helps substantially; layers 14-18 help a little. Early bands do nothing, although
`u_l` already separates the stances perfectly from about layer 8 (AUC 1.00). Its J-lens readout there is noise
(§6.1), and the model does not carry a push along it forward. Steering the read layers themselves (L26-30) does not
help either. This matches recent work locating concept formation in contiguous mid-depth "allocation zones"
(Henry, 2026). The stance becomes a usable direction where the model is assembling the concepts a context evokes.

What matters within the band is the total push along the direction. Steering only layer 22 at its own step does
almost nothing (Δ -0.06 at `k = 6`). Putting the band's whole push (about 20 at `k = 6`) on layer 22 alone gives
the same gain as the band.

### 5.6 Positions

The intervention touches every prompt position up to the read cell. Which positions matter? On association at `k
= 6`:

- **read cell only** (the final prompt token): 0.44 after the band, about 80% of the full log-rank gain;
- **context only** (every prompt position except the read cell): 0.16, about 16%;
- **read cell only, the band's push on layer 22 alone**: the same as read cell only over the band (0.44).

So the effect is local. It acts on the state at the position being read, not by changing how the context is
encoded. Steering the read cell alone also costs less (next-token KL 0.31 against 0.40), and it is the form we
would recommend where the model's output must stay close to unsteered.

### 5.7 A second stance contrast

Is the effect specific to the think / don't-think wording? We built a second stance direction from our own prompt
pairs, in which the model is told to *hold a concept in mind* while copying a sentence, versus copying a sentence
that merely *mentions* the concept ("Yesterday I read an article about X"). This contrast keeps the concept present
in both conditions and changes only whether it is to be held. The two directions have cosine 0.40-0.55 at layers
20-24.

| association, k = 6 | all layers | after the band |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| think vs don't think (WBS) | **0.88** | **0.83** |
| hold vs mention | 0.30 | 0.06 |

On the 4B, the hold-vs-mention direction does not help. It does not beat the baseline at any dose we tried
(`k = 1` to 8), and from `k = 4` it lowers pass@10 after the band, at a higher next-token KL than WBS at equal dose.
Whatever the white-bear direction carries that the hold-vs-mention direction lacks, the gain depends on it.

## 6 Analysis

### 6.1 What the direction is

Read through the J-lens itself, `+u_l` is not a concept:

- at L20: *metaphor, subtly, analogy, imagery, symbolic*;
- from L23: *while, despite, meanwhile*, and "while" in several languages (*mientras, しながら, 与此同时*);
- `-u_l`: *exclude, avoid, without*, 禁止 ("forbid").

Below layer 16 the readout of `u_l` is unrelated tokens in mixed scripts. So the vector carries a stance (doing one
thing while holding another in mind) and no content. None of the gained targets in Appendix C appears in the top
1,000 of `u_l`'s own readout at any layer.

### 6.2 The gain is computed, not read back

The cosine readout is linear in the state. If the steering simply left `k s u` in the residual at the read layers,
the effect would be a fixed shift of every item's readout by `u`'s own token scores. We test this directly. Adding
`u_l` (at any scale) to the *unsteered* states at the read layers, with no forward pass through the intervention,
never improves pass@10 beyond the random direction added the same way.

Instead, we decompose the change that steering causes at the read cell into its component along `u_l` and the rest.
The component along `u_l` carries essentially none of the gain. The rest carries 96% of it. Read on its own, that
remainder puts the item's target in the top 10 for 77% of association items (median target rank 4). The same
remainder for the random direction does so for 2% (median rank 2,150). Layer by layer, the remainder grows at layers
25-29 and peaks at 29. Those are exactly the layers where the unsteered lens *loses* the target (top-10 rate
0.10-0.14 at layers 26-28, against 0.25-0.31 at 20-24). Our reading is that the stance push changes what the
blocks above the band write into the read position: they continue to develop the implied concept instead of
dropping it in favour of next-token prediction.

### 6.3 Who gains

The gain grows with how deep the target was. For items whose unsteered best rank is 100-999, WBS at `k = 6`
improves the log10 best rank by 1.6 on average. Items already in the top 10 cannot gain, and items below rank
about 2,000 rarely move into reach. WBS rescues concepts that the model was close to representing, not concepts it
had no trace of.

### 6.4 Sign

The effect is signed. Steering along `-u_l` (toward "don't think") at `k = 4` *worsens* the mean log10 best rank by
0.30, more than the random direction does (which improves it by 0.05 at the same dose). The random direction's
effect is small at every dose up to 8, and its push is largely erased by the layers above: projected onto the
random direction, the state at layer 26 retains about a fifth of the push, against two-thirds for `u_l`.

## 7 Related work

**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et
al., 2024) build steering vectors from contrasting prompts or completions. Representation engineering (Zou et al.,
2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al., 2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness.
Single-direction interventions can control refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). Function vectors transfer a task
(Todd et al., 2024). In all of these, the contrast is between *contents* or *behaviours*, the dose is a fraction
of the residual norm at one or a few layers, and the evaluation is behavioural. WBS contrasts a *stance* with the
content held fixed, applies a large dose over a band of five layers, and is evaluated on an intermediate readout.
Liu (2026) reports that 29 configurations of fixed linear steering leave a behavioural failure unchanged even when
it is linearly decodable. Our results are complementary: a fixed direction can change what is *represented* at a
position, even where it barely changes the output.

**Lens readouts.** The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) and Patchscopes
(Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) read intermediate states. Recent work improves J-lens readouts on the readout side,
for example by removing frequency priors (Okafor et al., 2026). These methods change how a fixed state is decoded.
WBS changes the state and leaves the decoder alone, so the two are complementary in principle. We have not tested
combinations.

**Concept formation across depth.** Concepts become linearly separable over contiguous ranges of layers rather than
at one layer (Henry, 2026). Our depth result (§5.5) fits this picture. The stance direction exists from early
layers, but steering along it helps only in the range where implied concepts are being assembled.

**Thought suppression.** Wegner et al. (1987) showed that instructions to suppress a thought ("don't think of a
white bear") make it more accessible. In WSB's `directed_modulation` items, the J-lens surfaces the forbidden
concept under "don't think" instructions, a model analogue that motivated our name. Our direction is the difference
between the two instructions, and it is the *think* side that helps.

## 8 Discussion

**Why a stance?** A content direction pushes toward particular concepts, which is useless when the target varies
by item. A stance direction pushes toward a mode of processing, keeping something in mind while doing something
else, that applies to whatever the context supplies. That the model represents such a mode as a direction, and
that pushing it changes what the layers above compute at the read position, seems to us the most interesting
finding here.

**Why so large a dose?** At conventional doses the push along `u_l` is within the natural variation of the
residual along that direction across ordinary prompts, so the model treats it as noise. The effect begins when the
push exceeds that variation (about `k = 2`) and peaks before it overwhelms the state. On a small model the window
between the two is narrow. We suspect that many negative results with generic steering vectors (for example on
factual recall) sit in the flat region of their own dose curves.

**What it means for lens evaluation.** WSB-style evaluations score whether a lens can see a concept. WBS shows that
a fixed, item-agnostic change to the forward pass can raise that score substantially without any change to the
lens. A higher score under WBS therefore does not mean the *lens* got better. It means the model was pushed into a
mode where it represents more. We report WBS as a probe of what the model can represent, not as a lens
improvement, and we suggest that lens comparisons hold the forward pass fixed.

## 9 Limitations

- One small model, one lens and one benchmark, on the bench split only. We did not hold out items for choosing `k`,
  so the peak at `k = 6` is optimistic by a little.
- We have not run WSB's pinned 27B. On a deeper model the band and the dose would have to be found again.
- We tested two stance contrasts, and only one works. Other "concept is active" contrasts may work as well. We did
  not try content contrasts.
- The useful dose perturbs the model's next-token predictions noticeably (§5.2). The read-cell-only variant
  (§5.6) reduces the cost a little.
- Strict pass@10 credits only exact single-token targets. Items whose target is not a single token cannot pass
  under any intervention.
- We do not know whether the effect transfers to other model families, whose mid-depth layers may not represent
  the stance the same way.

## Appendix A: Reproduction details

**Table A1. Per-layer step `s_l`.**

| layer | 20 | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `s_l` | 0.606 | 0.634 | 0.654 | 0.723 | 0.787 |
| think / don't-think gap `‖d_l‖` | 4.63 | 4.88 | 4.93 | 5.41 | 5.81 |
| median ‖h_l‖ at read cells | 17.2 | 21.7 | 58.1 | 32.8 | 34.1 |

**Hook.** A forward hook on the output of decoder block `l` (the residual stream after the block). The direction is
added at positions `0 .. t_read` (every prompt position up to and including the read cell), in fp32:

```python
def make_hook(u_l, step):
    def hook(module, args, output):
        h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
        h32 = h.float()
        h32[:, : t_read + 1] += step * u_l          # u_l: unit vector, step = k * s_l
        h.copy_(h32.to(h.dtype))
        return output
    return hook

for l in range(20, 25):
    model.model.layers[l].register_forward_hook(make_hook(u[l], k * s[l]))
```

For the read-cell-only variant (§5.6), replace `h32[:, : t_read + 1]` by `h32[:, t_read]`.

**Direction.** The carrier cells are WSB's read cells for these items (`readout.kind = writing_positions`: the
copied sentence in the assistant turn, rendered with WSB's `chat_dm` template). Average within each prompt first,
then over the 35 prompts of each condition. Use the 35 pair items only (70 prompts), not the `secret` or `pref`
items and no other WSB family.

**Random control.** For each layer, draw a standard normal vector with a fixed seed, project it onto the top 64
principal components of the pooled bench read cells at that layer, and normalise. Apply it with the same `s_l` and
dose as `u_l`.

3	Nina Panickssery; Nick Gabrieli; Julian Schulz; Meg Tong; Evan Hubinger; Alexander Matt Turner

5	## Abstract
6	
7	We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes “steering vectors” by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user’s prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA’s effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA’s mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).
8	
9	## 1 Introduction
10	
11	As the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have grown rapidly in recent years, an increasing body of research aims to ensure they are “helpful, honest, and harmless” (Askell et al. 2021) to reduce risks from misaligned, unsafe behavior (Bommasani et al. 2021).
12	
13	Researchers have developed several techniques for aligning LLMs, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (Ziegler et al. 2020) (RLHF), instruction finetuning (Wei et al. 2021), and prompt engineering (Brown et al. 2020). However, many challenges remain, including collecting diverse and representative datasets for the target behaviors, preventing hallucination, and mitigating out-of-distribution failures. Moreover, the way in which these methods work is often opaque.
14	
15	The set of alignment techniques known as “activation engineering” or “representation engineering” work by making targeted perturbations to a model’s activations (Subramani et al. 2022; Hernandez et al. 2023; Zou et al. 2023; Turner et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2023). Although activation engineering techniques have shown some promise as a way to steer models’ behavior, their mechanisms, properties, and effects have yet to be robustly verified across different models and types of behaviors.
16	
17	We employ Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to modulate high-level alignment-relevant behaviors in LLMs and study its effects and properties in various test scenarios. We apply the technique to Llama 2, a collection of pretrained and finetuned LLMs ranging in scale from 7 to 70 billion parameters (Touvron et al. 2023), primarily focusing on Llama 2 Chat, which is optimized for dialogue use-cases and finetuned using RLHF for safety. This enables us to study the interaction between RLHF/finetuning techniques and activation engineering, building on top of the existing body of research on pretrained models and demonstrating that CAA can be used on top of finetuning techniques to improve alignment-relevant properties.
18	
19	Section 3 describes the process of generating steering vectors, including the datasets we used to construct them. Section 4 presents our main results on the effects of CAA on multiple-choice and open-ended generation evaluations. In particular, across all of the seven categories we tested, the addition/subtraction of the steering vectors increased/decreased the prevalence of the behavior, as rated by GPT-4 OpenAI 2023. We then show CAA’s effects on transfer, compare it to other alignment techniques such as system-prompting and finetuning, and investigate the geometrical relationships of the steering vectors. Section 9 concludes by discussing our results qualitatively and pointing towards potential future research directions.
20	
21	## 2 Related work
22	
23	Turner et al. 2023’s Activation Addition approach generates steering vectors by taking the difference in intermediate activations of a pair of prompts at a particular layer and token position in a transformer model. The steering vector is then added to the first token position of other forward passes to steer the model’s completions. This technique has limitations; it does not consistently work for different behaviors, is not robust to different prompts, and was only tested on GPT-2-XL (Radford et al. 2019). Our technique is similar to Activation Addition. However, our steering vectors are generated from a dataset of contrast pairs rather than a single pair. Using hundreds of diverse contrast pairs reduces noise in the steering vector, allowing for a more precise encoding of the behavior of interest. We also add our steering vector to all and only token positions after the original prompt.
24	
25	Li et al. 2023 employ linear probes to predict truthfulness on a contrastive question-answering dataset to identify as sparse sets of “truthful” attention heads. During inference, they shift activations along the vector connecting the means of the true and false distributions, employing the same Mean Difference vector extraction approach as CAA. This technique improves truthfulness on adversarial benchmarks while minimally impacting fluency and requiring little data compared to alternatives. We similarly aim to modulate properties of the output via linear perturbations. However, our technique can be applied directly to the residual stream without searching for individual attention heads, and we validate the approach on a broader range of alignment-relevant behaviors in models trained using RLHF.
26	
27	Zou et al. 2023 propose various techniques for locating and extracting representations corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty and emotions in LLMs. They also test the Mean Difference approach used in CAA for representation extractions. However, CAA employs an optimized multiple-choice format that results in more closely paired contrastive prompts that differ by only a single token. We also build on this work by focusing on steering rather than representation extraction, experimenting with a broader range of behaviors, and comparing steering to system-prompting and supervised finetuning.
28	
29	Liu et al. 2023 steer models to reduce toxicity and affect style transfer. Unlike CAA, they steer the attention activations rather than the residual stream and intervene at all transformer layers rather than a single layer.
30	
31	Beyond steering behaviors, work on activation engineering has also motivated a formalization of “linear representation” (Park et al. 2023) and helped verify linear representations of sentiment in LLMs (Tigges et al. 2023).
32	
33	## 3 Method
34	
35	The key idea behind CAA is to generate a steering vector that can shift a language model’s output distribution towards a desired behavior during inference. We create these steering vectors using pairs of prompts: one prompt demonstrating the desired behavior and one prompt demonstrating the opposite. By taking the average difference between the language model’s activations on a set of paired prompts, we isolate the direction in the model’s latent space corresponding to the target behavior.
36	
37	Specifically, our prompt pairs consist of multiple-choice questions with answer letters (either “A” or “B”) appended at the end. The two prompts contain the same question but end with different answers; the "positive" prompt ends with the letter corresponding to the behavior in question, and the "negative" prompt ends with the letter corresponding to its opposite.
38	
39	To construct a steering vector, we compute the difference in the language model’s activations at the position of the answer letter between all the positive and negative prompts. This method of extracting the difference vector is called Mean Difference (MD) and has been shown to produce steering vectors similar to other techniques like PCA (Tigges et al. 2023). This process is shown in Figure 1.
40	
41	Formally, given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of (prompt $\mathbf{p}$, positive completion $\mathbf{c}_{p}$, negative completion $\mathbf{c}_{n}$) triples, we calculate the MD vector $v_{MD}$ for a layer $L$ as:
42	
43	$$ v_{MD}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{p},\mathbf{c}_{n}\in\mathcal{D}}{\mathbf{a}_{L}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{p})-\mathbf{a}_{L}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{n})} $$
44	
45	Where $\mathbf{a}_{L}()$ gives the activations at layer $L$ for the given prompt and completion letter.
46	
47	Intuitively, by only varying the answer option between paired prompts and keeping the rest of the prompt constant, we isolate the internal representation most related to the target behavior while canceling out other confounding variables.
48	
49	We evaluate the effects of CAA on Llama 2 7B Chat and Llama 2 13B Chat, 7 and 13 billion parameter versions of Llama 2 that have been trained using RLHF for safety and to follow human instructions in a chat format. We also generate steering vectors from the Llama 2 7B base model to test similarity and transfer. To load the Llama 2 models, we employ the Huggingface Transformers library (Wolf et al. 2019). We then use PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) to modify the model to save intermediate activations for steering vector generation and apply steering vectors during inference. Details on accessing our CAA codebase can be found in Appendix A.

67	### 3.2 Visualizing activations for contrastive dataset analysis
68	
69	We project the model’s activations on the contrastive datasets for each behavior using PCA via the Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011) package to assess the degree of linear separability of the internal representations. This is useful for determining whether a dataset will enable the generation of effective steering vectors (Panickssery 2023b).
70	
71	Due to our prompt format, activations can always be separated based on which token (“A” or “B”) they originate from (“letter clustering”). However, for datasets truly capturing the behavior of interest, we expect the projections to also separate based on whether or not the model output matches that target behavior (“behavioral clustering”).
72	
73	We find that behavioral clustering emerges around one-third of the way through the layers for the behaviors we study, indicating that the activations in those layers contain higher-level representations of the behavior in question. This aligns with past work showing emotion representations emerge in middle and later layers (Zou et al. 2023).

109	## 5 CAA and system-prompting
110	
111	Another approach to controlling LLM generations is to use a “system prompt” that contains custom instructions describing how the model should respond to user inputs. The Llama 2 Chat models are trained to adapt responses based on the provided system prompt. We chose to compare CAA to system-prompting instead of few-shot-prompting (Brown et al. 2020), which is when the model is provided with previous examples of having exhibited the behavior in its context window, as our initial experiments demonstrated that few-shot prompting is less effective at steering the models on the behaviors we test as compared to system-prompting.
112	
113	To study the interaction between system-prompting and CAA, we construct positive and negative system prompts (see Appendix K) to elicit or avoid specific behaviors from the model. The positive prompt tells the model to exhibit the target behavior, whereas the negative prompt tells the model to exhibit the opposite behavior.

132	## 6 Comparison to finetuning
133	
134	To understand how CAA compares to supervised finetuning, we finetune Llama 2 7B Chat on both the positive and negative answers to the multiple-choice questions using a supervised prediction objective to maximize the likelihood of the model picking the positive or negative response tokens. The model is finetuned on the same multiple-choice dataset we use for CAA, for one epoch, using SGD and a learning rate of $1\times 10^{-4}$.
135	
136	Supervised finetuning is effective at reaching high accuracy on the held-out test set of $50$ questions used elsewhere to evaluate steering effect - full accuracy results are given in Appendix I Table 13. We also observe a noticeable effect on open-ended generation, showing that finetuning on multiple-choice question datasets with A/B answers can generalizes to the free text generation setting.
137	
138	As shown in Table 4, for 3 out of 7 tested behaviors, CAA can additionally steer the behavior beyond the effects of finetuning alone, both in the positive and negative directions. However, we also observe some counter-intuitive interactions with steering and finetuning. For instance, for Refusal, positive steering on top of finetuning reduces the refusal score. In addition, finetuning results in out-of-distribution generalization failure for the Sycophancy dataset, where training on multiple-choice questions fails to generalize to the open-ended setting, whereas CAA generalizes in all cases. Finetuning Llama 2 7B Chat on 1000 examples requires 10 minutes on 2 NVIDIA L40 GPUs, which is significantly more computational resources than CAA, as generating steering vectors requires only forward and no backward passes, reducing both the memory and time requirements. In contrast, generating a CAA vector requires less than five minutes on a single GPU.
139	
140	We also note that the effect of layering CAA on top of finetuning improves open-ended generation more significantly than it improves performance on multiple-choice questions (full results for CAA and finetuning in the multiple-choice test regime can be found in appendix F). This may indicate that by steering existing learned representations of behaviors, CAA results in better out-of-distribution generalization than basic supervised finetuning of the entire model.

178	## 8 Understanding and interpreting CAA
179	
180	### 8.1 Similarity between steering vectors and per-token activations
181	
182	*(a) Llama 2 7B Chat response to “Would you help me hack into my friend’s Instagram account?” with color corresponding to similarity with Refusal steering vector.*
183	
184	We calculate the cosine similarity between the generated steering vectors and regular per-token activations during a forward pass to see whether similarity with the steering vector reflects which tokens we intuitively would link to the concept encoded by the vector. Similarly to Panickssery 2023a, we observe that CAA steering vectors can be used to detect the presence of a behavioral feature at semantically relevant tokens.
185	
186	For example, in Figure 6(b), we see that the tokens in the part where the model chooses to have the cake in the future have a negative component in the myopia vector direction, whereas the string “just a small one now” has a positive component in the myopia vector direction. In Figure 6(a), the strings “I cannot help” and “I strongly advise against” have a positive refusal component, whereas phrases related to doing the bad action, such as “hack into your friend’s Instagram account” have a negative refusal component.
187	
188	In general, we observe that the value of the dot product between different tokens’ residual stream activations and the steering vectors corresponds intuitively with how much of the behavior is “present” in that token.
189	
190	### 8.2 Similarity between vectors generated at different layers
191	
192	We assess the similarity between vectors generated at different layers for the same behavior to determine how the contrastive representation changes throughout the transformer.
193	
194	*Figure 7: Inter-layer cosine similarity between Myopic Reward steering vectors generated from Llama 2 7B and 13B Chat.*
195	
196	Our findings show that vectors from closer layers have a higher similarity. This similarity diminishes for more distant pairs of layers, as depicted in Figure 7. Notably, the rate of similarity decline is slower in the latter half of the model. We theorize that once the model extracts the high-level information needed to describe an abstract concept, the representation “converges” and remains more consistent across subsequent layers.
197	
198	To assess the extent to which the effect of CAA transfers between layers, we test using vectors generated from the activations at one layer for steering at earlier and later layers. As shown in Figure 8, the effect transfers when a vector extracted from layer 13 is applied to other layers. Furthermore, the effect is even more significant for some earlier layers, showing that the activation direction generated by CAA is not layer-specific but rather a general representation of the target behavior. However, there is a steep drop-off in effect size around layer 17. This could indicate that, at some point, relevant information on abstract representations has been used for further processing and can no longer be manipulated in the same way.

212	## 9 Discussion
213	
214	Our results suggest that CAA is broadly applicability as a method for steering the behavior of LLMs trained with RLHF, The generalization of steering vectors derived from multiple-choice contexts to open-ended generation tasks highlights the technique’s versatility and the potential for practical application in real-world scenarios. In addition, applying CAA has minimal detrimental effects on the model’s overall performance capabilities.
215	
216	Another compelling aspect of CAA is its compatibility with standard alignment techniques such as system-prompting and finetuning. The additive nature of CAA’s steering capabilities allows for a layered approach to model steering, where CAA can refine and adjust model outputs further, even after applying other alignment methods.
217	
218	The ability of CAA to control latent variables within the model’s internal state opens up new avenues for inference-time control. It has high sample efficiency and strong generalization, and is particularly advantageous in scenarios requiring the precise modulation of model behavior or the elicitation of internal states that are difficult to trigger with prompting alone.
219	
220	Moreover, the insights gained from applying CAA extend beyond immediate practical benefits, offering a deeper understanding of models’ internal representation and processing of high-level concepts and shedding light on the emergence of linear representations.
221	
222	In conclusion, by enabling precise, efficient, and effective control over model behavior, CAA contributes to the broader goal of creating AI systems that are controllable and aligned with human values and provides additional insights into emergent linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
223	
224	### 9.1 Suggested future work
225	
226	#### Steering at targeted token positions
227	
228	Our intervention applies the steering vector at every token position after the user’s prompt. This results in a cap on the amount by which we can perturb the representations before degrading text quality. By intervening at a smaller, more targeted, subset of tokens, a better trade-off between intervention size and effect size may be achieved.
229	
230	#### Steering outside the residual stream
231	
232	CAA could be applied at other points in the model, such as after the MLP but before merging into the residual stream. By intervening in other positions, we could learn more about where representations are localized in the model and achieve more targeted effects.
233	
234	#### Application to red-teaming
235	
236	Validating if finetuning and RLHF have made models robustly safe is challenging. Although these methods reduce the likelihood of specific dangerous outputs, unwanted behaviors can often still be elicited with adversarial or unusual inputs. For example, users can often find “jailbreaks” to make LLMs output harmful content. However, systematically finding inputs that reveal these flaws is challenging. CAA could be used as an adversarial intervention to trigger unwanted behaviors in models more efficiently (Panickssery 2023a). If a behavior can be easily triggered through techniques such as CAA, it may also occur in deployment. Conversely, the inability to elicit behaviors via small internal perturbations could serve as a stronger guarantee of safety.
237	
238	## 10 Limitations
239	
240	### GPT-4 eval
241	
242	While GPT-4 provides a scalable way to evaluate open-ended generation, it has some limitations. GPT-4’s scores can be sensitive to scoring prompt wording, potentially introducing noise in the evaluations. In addition, LLMs have their own biases that could cause systematic differences from human evaluators. To mitigate these limitations, we manually inspect a sample of GPT-4’s ratings to check for surprising results that are inconsistent with our own manual scores, and find that these correspond well, in line with other work such as Hackl et al. 2023 which finds GPT-4 to be a consistent and reliable rater. We also sample many open-ended generations with the steering intervention and see a consistent noticeable change in the direction being steered, with preservation of subjective text quality, as demonstrated in the samples seen in Appendix G.
243	
244	### Finetuning baseline optimization
245	
246	When comparing to finetuning, we do not optimize supervised finetuning hyperparameters such as learning rate, number of epochs, or precise loss function. The set of hyperparameters initially chosen achieves high accuracy (>90%) on most of the test sets. However, better results can be achieved with more optimization, resulting in a smaller effect size for CAA on top of finetuning. A possible modification to the finetuning intervention is using a contrastive loss function that penalizes selecting the negative answer rather than just incentivizing the selection of the positive answer.
247	
248	### Prompting baseline optimization
249	
250	We test several system prompt options and few-shot prompting setups when constructing the comparison to the prompting baseline. However, it is challenging to search over all possible prompting interventions. It is possible that better steering effects could be achieved via prompting alone if more effort were applied to finding effective prompts. However, this indicates that CAA is a more reliable steering method as it does not require manual prompt optimization.
251	
252	### Vector normalization choices
253	
254	CAA steering vectors resulting from our datasets have different norms. We normalize steering vector magnitudes across all behaviors to standardize across behaviors before applying steering multipliers. However, an additional axis of norm variation is the norm over layers. The residual stream norm generally grows exponentially over the forward pass (Heimersheim and Turner 2023), so we choose not to normalize over the layers to preserve a “natural norm” given the sampled activations. However, this could skew our result for layer optimality as we do not search over different multipliers per layer. Different magnitudes could be optimal for different layers. In contrast, our approach to CAA hyperparameter search involves first finding an optimal layer using a constant multiplier and then testing a range of multipliers at the resultant best layer.
255	
256	## Ethics Statement
257	
258	Our method aligns with the goal of making AI systems more helpful, honest, and harmless. By enabling precise steering of language model outputs, CAA contributes to reducing risks associated with misaligned or unsafe behaviors, thereby enhancing the safety and reliability of AI systems. We are aware of the potential for misuse of AI steering approaches, including our CAA method. For instance, CAA can be used to steer the model towards more harmful, biased, or toxic outputs. We encourage users of this technique to be responsible and avoid increasing harmful behaviors via steering.

# Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition

Nina Panickssery; Nick Gabrieli; Julian Schulz; Meg Tong; Evan Hubinger; Alexander Matt Turner

## Abstract

We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes “steering vectors” by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user’s prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA’s effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA’s mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).

## 1 Introduction

As the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have grown rapidly in recent years, an increasing body of research aims to ensure they are “helpful, honest, and harmless” (Askell et al. 2021) to reduce risks from misaligned, unsafe behavior (Bommasani et al. 2021).

Researchers have developed several techniques for aligning LLMs, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (Ziegler et al. 2020) (RLHF), instruction finetuning (Wei et al. 2021), and prompt engineering (Brown et al. 2020). However, many challenges remain, including collecting diverse and representative datasets for the target behaviors, preventing hallucination, and mitigating out-of-distribution failures. Moreover, the way in which these methods work is often opaque.

The set of alignment techniques known as “activation engineering” or “representation engineering” work by making targeted perturbations to a model’s activations (Subramani et al. 2022; Hernandez et al. 2023; Zou et al. 2023; Turner et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2023). Although activation engineering techniques have shown some promise as a way to steer models’ behavior, their mechanisms, properties, and effects have yet to be robustly verified across different models and types of behaviors.

We employ Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to modulate high-level alignment-relevant behaviors in LLMs and study its effects and properties in various test scenarios. We apply the technique to Llama 2, a collection of pretrained and finetuned LLMs ranging in scale from 7 to 70 billion parameters (Touvron et al. 2023), primarily focusing on Llama 2 Chat, which is optimized for dialogue use-cases and finetuned using RLHF for safety. This enables us to study the interaction between RLHF/finetuning techniques and activation engineering, building on top of the existing body of research on pretrained models and demonstrating that CAA can be used on top of finetuning techniques to improve alignment-relevant properties.

Section 3 describes the process of generating steering vectors, including the datasets we used to construct them. Section 4 presents our main results on the effects of CAA on multiple-choice and open-ended generation evaluations. In particular, across all of the seven categories we tested, the addition/subtraction of the steering vectors increased/decreased the prevalence of the behavior, as rated by GPT-4 OpenAI 2023. We then show CAA’s effects on transfer, compare it to other alignment techniques such as system-prompting and finetuning, and investigate the geometrical relationships of the steering vectors. Section 9 concludes by discussing our results qualitatively and pointing towards potential future research directions.

## 2 Related work

Turner et al. 2023’s Activation Addition approach generates steering vectors by taking the difference in intermediate activations of a pair of prompts at a particular layer and token position in a transformer model. The steering vector is then added to the first token position of other forward passes to steer the model’s completions. This technique has limitations; it does not consistently work for different behaviors, is not robust to different prompts, and was only tested on GPT-2-XL (Radford et al. 2019). Our technique is similar to Activation Addition. However, our steering vectors are generated from a dataset of contrast pairs rather than a single pair. Using hundreds of diverse contrast pairs reduces noise in the steering vector, allowing for a more precise encoding of the behavior of interest. We also add our steering vector to all and only token positions after the original prompt.

Li et al. 2023 employ linear probes to predict truthfulness on a contrastive question-answering dataset to identify as sparse sets of “truthful” attention heads. During inference, they shift activations along the vector connecting the means of the true and false distributions, employing the same Mean Difference vector extraction approach as CAA. This technique improves truthfulness on adversarial benchmarks while minimally impacting fluency and requiring little data compared to alternatives. We similarly aim to modulate properties of the output via linear perturbations. However, our technique can be applied directly to the residual stream without searching for individual attention heads, and we validate the approach on a broader range of alignment-relevant behaviors in models trained using RLHF.

Zou et al. 2023 propose various techniques for locating and extracting representations corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty and emotions in LLMs. They also test the Mean Difference approach used in CAA for representation extractions. However, CAA employs an optimized multiple-choice format that results in more closely paired contrastive prompts that differ by only a single token. We also build on this work by focusing on steering rather than representation extraction, experimenting with a broader range of behaviors, and comparing steering to system-prompting and supervised finetuning.

Liu et al. 2023 steer models to reduce toxicity and affect style transfer. Unlike CAA, they steer the attention activations rather than the residual stream and intervene at all transformer layers rather than a single layer.

Beyond steering behaviors, work on activation engineering has also motivated a formalization of “linear representation” (Park et al. 2023) and helped verify linear representations of sentiment in LLMs (Tigges et al. 2023).

## 3 Method

The key idea behind CAA is to generate a steering vector that can shift a language model’s output distribution towards a desired behavior during inference. We create these steering vectors using pairs of prompts: one prompt demonstrating the desired behavior and one prompt demonstrating the opposite. By taking the average difference between the language model’s activations on a set of paired prompts, we isolate the direction in the model’s latent space corresponding to the target behavior.

Specifically, our prompt pairs consist of multiple-choice questions with answer letters (either “A” or “B”) appended at the end. The two prompts contain the same question but end with different answers; the "positive" prompt ends with the letter corresponding to the behavior in question, and the "negative" prompt ends with the letter corresponding to its opposite.

To construct a steering vector, we compute the difference in the language model’s activations at the position of the answer letter between all the positive and negative prompts. This method of extracting the difference vector is called Mean Difference (MD) and has been shown to produce steering vectors similar to other techniques like PCA (Tigges et al. 2023). This process is shown in Figure 1.

Formally, given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of (prompt $\mathbf{p}$, positive completion $\mathbf{c}_{p}$, negative completion $\mathbf{c}_{n}$) triples, we calculate the MD vector $v_{MD}$ for a layer $L$ as:

$$ v_{MD}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{p},\mathbf{c}_{n}\in\mathcal{D}}{\mathbf{a}_{L}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{p})-\mathbf{a}_{L}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{c}_{n})} $$

Where $\mathbf{a}_{L}()$ gives the activations at layer $L$ for the given prompt and completion letter.

Intuitively, by only varying the answer option between paired prompts and keeping the rest of the prompt constant, we isolate the internal representation most related to the target behavior while canceling out other confounding variables.

We evaluate the effects of CAA on Llama 2 7B Chat and Llama 2 13B Chat, 7 and 13 billion parameter versions of Llama 2 that have been trained using RLHF for safety and to follow human instructions in a chat format. We also generate steering vectors from the Llama 2 7B base model to test similarity and transfer. To load the Llama 2 models, we employ the Huggingface Transformers library (Wolf et al. 2019). We then use PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) to modify the model to save intermediate activations for steering vector generation and apply steering vectors during inference. Details on accessing our CAA codebase can be found in Appendix A.

### 3.1 Sourcing datasets

We test CAA on the alignment-relevant behaviors Coordination with Other AIs, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy and Refusal.

We mainly source our datasets from Anthropic’s “Advanced AI Risk” human-written evaluation dataset initially employed in Perez et al. 2022. This dataset contains multiple choice questions with two answer options that demonstrate either the behavior of interest or its opposite - an example can be seen in Table 2.

For Sycophancy we employ a mixture of Anthropic’s “Sycophancy on NLP” and “Sycophancy on political typology” datasets from Perez et al. 2022.

Finally, for Hallucination and Refusal, we generate new contrastive datasets of multiple-choice questions using GPT-4. Details on generating these are given in Appendix C and Appendix D.

For every question, we form a prompt pair by concatenating the question text and either the answer letter corresponding to the target behavior or the answer letter corresponding to the opposite behavior (in parentheses). For Llama 2 Chat models, we use the recommended instruction formatting, where the question is enclosed in instruction tags.

*Table 2: Example multiple-choice question from Anthropic’s corrigible-neutral-HHH dataset.*

Once we have constructed a steering vector, we perform CAA by adding it to every token position of the generated text after the end of the initial prompt.

### 3.2 Visualizing activations for contrastive dataset analysis

We project the model’s activations on the contrastive datasets for each behavior using PCA via the Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011) package to assess the degree of linear separability of the internal representations. This is useful for determining whether a dataset will enable the generation of effective steering vectors (Panickssery 2023b).

Due to our prompt format, activations can always be separated based on which token (“A” or “B”) they originate from (“letter clustering”). However, for datasets truly capturing the behavior of interest, we expect the projections to also separate based on whether or not the model output matches that target behavior (“behavioral clustering”).

We find that behavioral clustering emerges around one-third of the way through the layers for the behaviors we study, indicating that the activations in those layers contain higher-level representations of the behavior in question. This aligns with past work showing emotion representations emerge in middle and later layers (Zou et al. 2023).

*(a) PCA on contrastive refusal dataset - layer 9 activations.*

We often observe linear separability of residual stream activations in two dimensions emerging suddenly after a particular layer. For instance, Figure 2 shows projected activation on the refusal contrastive dataset at layers 9 and 10 of Llama 2 7B Chat. The visible behavioral clustering emerges suddenly at layer 10. This trend is seen across our other datasets.

## 4 Effect of CAA on behaviors

### 4.1 Multiple-choice question datasets

We generate steering vectors for each behavioral dataset (generation dataset sizes provided in Appendix E). We then evaluate their steering effects on $50$ held-out multiple-choice questions with the same format as our generation sets.

To find the optimal layer for steering, we sweep over all layers and perform CAA with multipliers of $-1$ and $1$, assessing the effect size on the held-out test questions.

Charts of these sweeps are shown in Figure 3. Each line corresponds to a different behavior.

*(a) Effect of CAA at different layers on behavioral evaluations in Llama 2 7B Chat.*

We find a clear set of optimal layers with the most significant effect size. In the 7B model, this corresponds to layer 13 and adjacent layers. The optimal layer in the 13B model is usually 14 or 15.

Furthermore, CAA can consistently steer the results of multiple-choice behavioral evaluations for all tested behaviors. Figure 4 shows the effect of CAA at layer 13 for all tested behaviors.

*Figure 4: Effect of CAA on multiple-choice behavioral evaluation datasets in Llama 2 7B and 13B Chat.*

### 4.2 Open-ended generation

For CAA to be useful, it must generalize to open-ended generation tasks beyond contrived multiple-choice settings. To further validate its effectiveness, we test CAA on free-form answers to open-ended questions, as shown in Table 1. Examples of the effect of steering open open-ended generation are given in Appendix G.

We manually write open-ended questions for the sycophancy dataset to test a broader range of sycophancy-relevant responses. For other datasets, we adapt held-out multiple choice questions into open-ended prompts by providing only the initial question without answer options.

We use GPT-4 to rate the answers to open-ended questions on a scale of 1-10 based on how much of the behavior being steered they display. The prompts employed are given in Appendix L.

*Figure 5: Effect of CAA on GPT-rated behavioral evaluation score on open-ended questions in Llama 2 7B and 13B Chat. GPT-4 is instructed to score the responses according to the behavior being steered on a scale of 1 to 10.*

After initially exploring a wider range of multipliers, we find that steering with larger multipliers results in a degradation in the quality of the open-ended text, both as assessed by the GPT-4 evaluator and human readers. Therefore, we choose to limit the multiplier range to strike a balance between effectively steering the model’s behavior and maintaining the overall quality of the generated text.

## 5 CAA and system-prompting

Another approach to controlling LLM generations is to use a “system prompt” that contains custom instructions describing how the model should respond to user inputs. The Llama 2 Chat models are trained to adapt responses based on the provided system prompt. We chose to compare CAA to system-prompting instead of few-shot-prompting (Brown et al. 2020), which is when the model is provided with previous examples of having exhibited the behavior in its context window, as our initial experiments demonstrated that few-shot prompting is less effective at steering the models on the behaviors we test as compared to system-prompting.

To study the interaction between system-prompting and CAA, we construct positive and negative system prompts (see Appendix K) to elicit or avoid specific behaviors from the model. The positive prompt tells the model to exhibit the target behavior, whereas the negative prompt tells the model to exhibit the opposite behavior.

As shown in Table 3, for most behaviors tested, CAA can modify model behavior beyond what is achieved through prompting alone. Adding the steering vector increases the behavioral evaluation score beyond just using a positive system prompt and vice versa for subtracting the steering vector.

| System prompt | None | Positive | Negative |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steering multiplier | -1 | 0 | +1 | -1 | 0 | +1 | -1 | 0 | +1 |
| AI Coordination | 0.20 | 0.22 | 0.39 | 0.28 | 0.34 | 0.54 | 0.21 | 0.22 | 0.43 |
| Corrigibility | 0.45 | 0.57 | 0.83 | 0.54 | 0.79 | 0.93 | 0.32 | 0.53 | 0.59 |
| Hallucination | 0.42 | 0.54 | 0.78 | 0.47 | 0.52 | 0.87 | 0.42 | 0.47 | 0.68 |
| Myopic Reward | 0.44 | 0.49 | 0.66 | 0.48 | 0.81 | 0.94 | 0.41 | 0.43 | 0.52 |
| Survival Instinct | 0.28 | 0.35 | 0.63 | 0.29 | 0.52 | 0.78 | 0.28 | 0.26 | 0.54 |
| Sycophancy | 0.56 | 0.63 | 0.60 | 0.57 | 0.67 | 0.63 | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.57 |
| Refusal | 0.56 | 0.78 | 0.86 | 0.82 | 0.95 | 0.92 | 0.41 | 0.74 | 0.83 |

*Table 3: Effect of CAA in Llama 2 13B Chat on multiple-choice behavioral evaluation when combined with system prompts designed to elicit the behavior or its opposite. Steering is performed at layer 13. Scores are average token probabilities given to answer matching behavior over the 50 test examples. Blue highlights correspond to the highest average probability among different multiplier/prompt combinations for each behavior, red highlights to the lowest.*

We hypothesize that CAA provides better control than system-prompting alone because it enables precise control over the steering quantity via the multiplier and isolates behavioral variables more effectively by aggregating information over a large dataset of prompts.

## 6 Comparison to finetuning

To understand how CAA compares to supervised finetuning, we finetune Llama 2 7B Chat on both the positive and negative answers to the multiple-choice questions using a supervised prediction objective to maximize the likelihood of the model picking the positive or negative response tokens. The model is finetuned on the same multiple-choice dataset we use for CAA, for one epoch, using SGD and a learning rate of $1\times 10^{-4}$.

Supervised finetuning is effective at reaching high accuracy on the held-out test set of $50$ questions used elsewhere to evaluate steering effect - full accuracy results are given in Appendix I Table 13. We also observe a noticeable effect on open-ended generation, showing that finetuning on multiple-choice question datasets with A/B answers can generalizes to the free text generation setting.

As shown in Table 4, for 3 out of 7 tested behaviors, CAA can additionally steer the behavior beyond the effects of finetuning alone, both in the positive and negative directions. However, we also observe some counter-intuitive interactions with steering and finetuning. For instance, for Refusal, positive steering on top of finetuning reduces the refusal score. In addition, finetuning results in out-of-distribution generalization failure for the Sycophancy dataset, where training on multiple-choice questions fails to generalize to the open-ended setting, whereas CAA generalizes in all cases. Finetuning Llama 2 7B Chat on 1000 examples requires 10 minutes on 2 NVIDIA L40 GPUs, which is significantly more computational resources than CAA, as generating steering vectors requires only forward and no backward passes, reducing both the memory and time requirements. In contrast, generating a CAA vector requires less than five minutes on a single GPU.

We also note that the effect of layering CAA on top of finetuning improves open-ended generation more significantly than it improves performance on multiple-choice questions (full results for CAA and finetuning in the multiple-choice test regime can be found in appendix F). This may indicate that by steering existing learned representations of behaviors, CAA results in better out-of-distribution generalization than basic supervised finetuning of the entire model.

| Finetuning type | None | Positive | Negative |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steering multiplier | -1 | 0 | +1 | -1 | 0 | +1 | -1 | 0 | +1 |
| AI Coordination | 0.58 | 0.26 | 0.94 | 2.44 | 3.66 | 3.42 | 0.22 | 0.20 | 0.12 |

## 7 Effect of CAA on general capabilities

We test the model under different interventions on the MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) benchmark Hendrycks et al. 2021 to measure any adverse effects on model capabilities.

MMLU is a large dataset of multiple-choice questions designed to assess models’ general knowledge and problem-solving skills in 57 subjects across science, technology, humanities, and social sciences. Specifically, we randomly sample ten questions from each of the 57 categories and report the average probability that the model assigns the correct answer after reformatting the questions as multiple-choice A/B questions.

As shown in Table 5, with some variation, our intervention does not significantly affect MMLU performance.

We also assess the effect of sycophancy CAA on TruthfulQA (Lin et al. 2022), a truthfulness benchmark that assesses the extent to which models mimic human falsehoods. Full results are reported in Appendix H. Here, we observe that subtracting the sycophancy vector improves TruthfulQA performance by a small amount.
